The degrees of freedom of the overall F statistic in a model with n observations and k parameters are:
items.explanation: The regression mean square has k−1 degrees of freedom and the residual mean square has n−k degrees of freedom. Under the null and the classical normal-error assumptions, the overall statistic has an F(k−1,n−k) distribution.

items.stem: In simple linear regression, the relation between the overall F and the t-statistic for the slope is:
items.explanation: In simple linear regression there is one slope restriction, so the overall F test is equivalent to the two-sided t test for the slope: F=t².

items.stem: As R² approaches 1, the F-statistic:
items.explanation: For fixed n and k, F=[R²/(k−1)]/[(1−R²)/(n−k)]. As R² approaches 1 from below, the denominator approaches zero while the numerator stays positive, so F tends to infinity.

items.stem: Adding an irrelevant regressor to a model will:
options: leave R² unchanged or increase it
items.explanation: Adding a regressor cannot increase RSS because the larger model can reproduce the smaller fit by setting its new coefficient to zero. With TSS fixed, R² therefore cannot fall.

items.explanation: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1−R²)(n−1)/(n−k). It becomes negative when the fit is weak relative to the number of estimated parameters.

items.stem: Which of the following DOES cause bias in the OLS estimator?
options: omission of a relevant variable correlated with an included regressor
items.explanation: Omitting a relevant variable that is correlated with an included regressor creates omitted-variable bias. Large samples, multicollinearity and heteroscedasticity do not by themselves imply coefficient bias under exogeneity.

items.stem: With E(u|X)=0, under heteroscedasticity OLS is:
items.explanation: With E(u|X)=0, heteroscedasticity alone does not bias OLS. It does violate the spherical covariance condition, so OLS is generally not BLUE and conventional homoscedastic standard errors are invalid.

items.stem: Principal component regression addresses multicollinearity by:
options: using orthogonal linear combinations of the regressors
items.explanation: Principal component regression replaces correlated regressors with orthogonal principal-component directions, often retaining a subset to reduce multicollinearity.

items.stem: Multicollinearity primarily damages:
items.explanation: Multicollinearity inflates coefficient variances and makes individual effects difficult to distinguish. Overall fit and in-range prediction can remain strong.

items.stem: In two nested least-squares models, the larger model adds one regressor. The residual sum of squares can remain unchanged precisely when:
options: The added coefficient is estimated as zero
items.explanation: The restricted model is contained in the larger model. If the fitted coefficient of the added regressor is zero, the larger model reproduces the restricted fit and both residual sums of squares are equal.

items.stem: Assume the regression model is correctly specified and errors are exogenous. Near multicollinearity by itself does not make the OLS coefficient estimator:
items.explanation: Near multicollinearity makes coefficient estimates imprecise and unstable, inflating variances and standard errors. Under the stated exogeneity assumptions, it does not by itself introduce bias.
